title: The first Berlin performance and the cry of 'Bis'
summary: Before the opening, Lenidow depends on Wooding; the stunned silence after the overture is followed by 'bis' which they mistake for 'beasts'.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Tell me about the first performance.

Well, the first performance was -- well, Lenidow come and give me a pep talk, you see. He said, "Well Sam, it all depends on you now." We were getting ready to go into the pit. He said, -- and I said, in my brave voice that was shaking and all like that, I said to him, "Well, don't worry, Mr. Lenidow," Dr. Lenidow, we used to call him, "we'll make it. Everything will be alright." (laugh) And I was shaking worse than he was. Because he was trying something, neither one knew that it was going to be a success.
Now, when we started playing. The band just set there and when he give me the signal to start in, I tapped the baton and we started what we used for an overture, "By the Waters of the Minnetonka".

And see, now, the people were -- everybody, everything was quiet, see. Because they don't know what we -- whether we're going to jump up and grab the chandeliers or not. They don't know what's going to happen. So we started off. When we finished this number, everything, for about two or three seconds, nothing happened. Everybody set there, (sings). And see,

we said, 'Oh, god, what's happening here.' The American propaganda had been so tough on the Kaiser and that, we didn't know whether they were ready to turn us into sausage or not, you see. So, but, and then when they did start, they started hollering, 'Bis, Bis'. Well, we thought they were saying 'beasts'. They were saying 'bis', encore. But it sounded like to me, they were calling us beasts, b-e-a-s-t.
So, the saxophone, being on this side, they were near the entrance to the pit. They had their horns, one of them was halfway -- they had the door open to the pit, going out.

Getting back in there because they expected things to -- and then suddenly, must have been an American or somebody that had been to America, said, 'Encore'. And I hollered, 'Hey, fellas, come back.' (laugh) (unintelligible), because we didn't know -- because they had done bad propaganda against the German people and we thought that we was taking a chance even being over there. That's the reason a lot of people didn't come in with the show. In 1925, and here with all this propaganda from the first world war.

So, what happened, when we got back in there, then they applauded and they started stomping their feet, see. And hollered, 'Encore, encore.'
